subject: Ophthalmology
title: Glaucoma: Primary Open-Angle vs Acute Angle-Closure
preview: Distinguish slowly progressive open-angle glaucoma from acute symptomatic angle closure, an ocular emergency.

sections.title: Recognize the two major presentations
points: Open-angle glaucoma can produce optic disc cupping and characteristic visual-field defects.
Acute angle closure may produce corneal haze, a mid-dilated pupil and markedly elevated intraocular pressure, warranting emergency ophthalmic assessment.

sections.title: Assessment and treatment principles
points: Evaluate intraocular pressure, optic nerve, visual field and angle anatomy as indicated.
Angle closure requires urgent eye-pressure reduction and definitive angle management by an ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Normal-range measured pressure does not rule out every form of glaucoma.
Do not delay treatment of acute painful vision loss while waiting for outpatient investigations.

quickRevision: Glaucoma causes progressive optic nerve damage; intraocular pressure is an important risk factor but a single pressure value is not the diagnosis.
Open-angle disease often progresses without pain or obvious early vision symptoms.
Acute angle closure may present with severe ocular pain, red eye, halos, nausea and rapid visual deterioration.

quiz.question: Which glaucoma subtype may present with sudden severe pain and halos?
options: Stable open-angle glaucoma without acute event
quiz.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma. Acute angle closure may produce corneal haze, a mid-dilated pupil and markedly elevated intraocular pressure, warranting emergency ophthalmic assessment.
